title: Why Cosy Mysteries Belong on Branch Lines
body:
A cosy needs a community small enough that everyone matters and a rhythm that lets secrets keep for years. A railway town gives both: the timetable orders the day, the station orders the town, and every arrival is noticed. The Timetable Cipher grew out of that geometry.

The trains are not decoration. Timings are alibis, delays are clues, and a stationmaster's library — with its ledgers and lost-property register — turns out to be the perfect archive for a mystery.

title: Ciphers, Timetables and the Appeal of Solvable Puzzles
body:
The cipher in the title is genuine — solvable with the book in hand — because cosy readers like to play along. The rule I hold to is that every puzzle must be fair and every solution must matter to a person, not just to the plot.

A code that only exists to be clever is a crossword. A code that hides why a woman left town in 1962 is a story.

title: The Tearoom Scene: Small Talk as Interrogation
body:
Half the detective work in a cosy happens over tea. The craft is in letting characters reveal things sideways — through what they complain about, what they don't mention, whose cup they refill. Direct questions are for the police; my detectives listen.

Readers say these scenes are the ones they remember. They are also the hardest to write, because nothing can be allowed to sound like exposition.
